papers.title: Targeting protein degradation strategies in drug discovery: integrating PROTACs, ubiquitination biology, and AI-driven design.
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy for eliminating disease-associated proteins, including targets that remain challenging to modulate using conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors. Among TPD approaches, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) exploit the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) to induce selective and event-driven degradation of proteins of interest (POIs). Despite rapid advances in PROTAC development, successful translation depends on interconnected determinants, including target degradability, ubiquitin ligase (E3) recruitment,
papers.summary: This review examines targeted protein degradation as a therapeutic strategy, focusing on PROTACs that hijack the ubiquitin-proteasome system to eliminate disease-causing proteins rather than merely inhibiting them. It discusses key determinants of successful PROTAC translation—including target degradability and E3 ligase recruitment—and how AI-driven design is being integrated into the field. The paper synthesizes ubiquitination biology with drug discovery approaches to guide future development.

papers.title: canSAR 2026-an update to the public drug discovery knowledgebase.
papers.abstract: canSAR (https://cansar.ai) serves as the world's largest public platform for cancer drug discovery and translational research. It serves as an exploration and hypothesis generation platform for drug discovery through (i) fully integrating large, multidisciplinary data from public resources, as well as bespoke curated data, creating a connected, navigable drug discovery knowledge map; and (ii) applying a suite of machine learning and AI tools to generate novel insights. We share the latest updates to canSAR highlighting growth across all data, enhancements to the predictive algorithms, and cont
papers.summary: canSAR 2026 is an updated release of the world's largest public knowledgebase for cancer drug discovery and translational research. It integrates multidisciplinary public and curated data into a connected knowledge map and adds enhanced machine learning and AI tools for generating novel drug discovery insights. The update highlights growth across all data types and improvements to predictive algorithms.

papers.title: DGIdb in 2026: an interoperable resource for the druggable genome.
papers.abstract: The Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb; https://dgidb.org) is an open-access aggregate knowledgebase that normalizes and centralizes drug-gene interaction and gene annotation data from diverse therapeutic and biomedical sources. Since its previous update, DGIdb has expanded its data content and added new tooling to better support programmatic access and local deployment. This release updates existing sources and incorporates three new sources of interaction data, including annotation data from the Molecular Oncology Almanac, the PRISM Repurposing Dataset, and the Broad Institute Drug Repurp
papers.summary: DGIdb 2026 is an updated open-access knowledgebase that aggregates and normalizes drug-gene interaction data from many sources, now adding three new datasets (Molecular Oncology Almanac, PRISM Repurposing, and Broad Institute Drug Repurposing). The release also improves programmatic access and local deployment options, making it easier for researchers to integrate druggable-genome data into their own pipelines.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in basic and translational cardiovascular research.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in cardiovascular research where conventional analysis struggles with scale, heterogeneity, and multimodal integration. Its contribution differs across imaging, computational omics, mechanistic simulation, and drug discovery. This narrative review examines substantive applications of machine learning and deep learning while distinguishing them from routine bioinformatics and purely biophysical modeling. We assess independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference in representative studies. Deep-learning imaging syste
papers.summary: This narrative review surveys how machine learning and deep learning are being applied across cardiovascular research, from medical imaging and computational omics to mechanistic simulation and drug discovery. It emphasizes the need to distinguish genuine AI contributions from routine bioinformatics and purely biophysical modeling, and it evaluates studies based on independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference. The review is aimed at helping researchers judge the rigor and translational potential of AI-based cardiovascular studies.

papers.title: Design, synthesis, and docking analysis of benzene sulfonamide-[1,4]benzoxazepine hybrids as acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase inhibitors.
papers.abstract: A series of novel hybrid [1,4]benzoxazepine-based sulfonamide derivatives 9-12a-j were synthesized and evaluated for their inhibitory activity against acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE). Compounds 9a and 9b exhibited potent dual cholinesterase inhibition, with IC50 values of 9.04 and 8.61 µM against AChE and 3.08 and 4.64 µM against BChE, respectively. Compound 12j emerged as the most potent BChE inhibitor of the series (IC50 = 1.06 ± 0.11 µM), displaying pronounced BChE preference (SI = 10.37), whereas 9d showed the highest BChE selectivity (BChE IC50 = 4.18 ± 0.56 µ
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a series of hybrid [1,4]benzoxazepine-sulfonamide compounds and tested them as inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), enzymes targeted in Alzheimer's disease therapy. Several compounds showed micromolar dual inhibition, with compound 12j being the most potent BChE inhibitor (IC50 = 1.06 µM) and compound 9d showing the greatest BChE selectivity. Docking analysis was used to rationalize binding interactions.

papers.title: Toll-Like Receptors in Mycoplasma Infections: Immunopathogenesis, Cheminformatics, and Machine Learning-Based Insights into TLR-Targeted Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Mycoplasma species are the minimal-genome pathogens that elicit complex host immune responses involving both protective and pathogenic inflammation. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pivotal components of the immune system, recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns to initiate immune responses. TLRs recognize Mycoplasma-derived lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA motifs, initiating NF-κB and MAPK signaling cascades. While these pathways are indispensable for microbial clearance, their dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, auto
papers.summary: This review examines how Toll-like receptors recognize Mycoplasma components such as lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA, triggering NF-κB and MAPK signaling that can drive both protective immunity and chronic inflammatory pathology. The authors integrate cheminformatics and machine-learning approaches to identify and prioritize potential TLR-targeted therapeutic compounds for Mycoplasma infections. The work bridges immunopathogenesis with computational drug-discovery strategies for these minimal-genome pathogens.

papers.title: AI-powered virtual cells, digital twins and agentic AI are reshaping multi-omics, spatial biology and drug discovery.
papers.abstract: Predicting individual disease trajectories and treatment responses remains challenging in drug discovery. Molecular profiling provides static snapshots that miss cellular dynamics, spatial context and adaptive responses. The convergence of single-cell and spatial omics with generative AI is driving a paradigm shift toward AI-powered virtual cells that model cellular states, interactions and treatment responses.
papers.summary: This perspective argues that combining single-cell and spatial omics with generative AI is enabling a new class of 'virtual cell' and 'digital twin' models that capture cellular dynamics, spatial context, and adaptive treatment responses rather than static molecular snapshots. The authors frame this convergence, alongside agentic AI, as a paradigm shift for multi-omics analysis and drug discovery, particularly for predicting individual disease trajectories and treatment outcomes.

papers.title: From static structures to conformational ensembles: Artificial intelligence for protein sampling and dynamics.
papers.abstract: After sparking a revolution in protein structure prediction, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) are now reshaping the modeling of protein conformational ensembles and dynamics. A fast, scalable, and accurate representation of protein conformational ensembles could enable genome-scale studies of protein function, with broad applications in drug discovery and protein engineering. The challenges associated with this goal, however, are far greater than those involved in single structure prediction because of the broad timescales spanned by protein motion, the complex relations
papers.summary: This review discusses how machine learning and AI are moving beyond static protein structure prediction to modeling protein conformational ensembles and dynamics. It highlights the potential for fast, scalable ensemble representations to enable genome-scale studies of protein function, while noting the greater challenges posed by the broad timescales and complex relationships involved in protein motion.

papers.title: Synthesis and antiproliferative screening of para-halogenated 4H-chromene-benzene hybrids: crystallographic, and molecular-docking studies.
papers.abstract: A series of novel 4H-chromene-benzene hybrids bearing para-halogen substituents (F, Cl, Br, I) on the phenyl moiety were efficiently synthesized via an ultrasonic-assisted one-pot three-component cyclocondensation reaction. The reaction proceeded in 93-96% yield within 2 minutes under mild conditions. The structures were fully characterized by IR, 1D/2D NMR, mass spectrometry, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction of 4b. The antiproliferative activity of all compounds was evaluated against twelve human cancer cell lines using the MTT assay. Compound 4b (4-Cl) exhibited the most broadly active p
papers.summary: This paper reports a fast, high-yield synthesis of 4H-chromene-benzene hybrids with para-halogen substituents, using an ultrasonic-assisted one-pot reaction that completes in 2 minutes with 93-96% yield. The compounds were structurally characterized, including by X-ray crystallography, and screened for antiproliferative activity against twelve human cancer cell lines. The 4-chloro derivative (4b) showed the broadest activity, with molecular docking used to explore possible binding interactions.

papers.title: Machine learning for small-molecule antibiotics - discovery to pre-clinical optimization.
papers.abstract: The rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health crisis, with 4.71 million associated deaths and 1.14 million attributable deaths in 2021. By 2050, these tolls are forecasted to rise to 8.22 million associated deaths and 1.91 million attributable deaths annually. Despite this growing burden, the antibacterial pipeline is alarmingly lean, with few candidates exhibiting truly novel mechanisms of action (MOA). This innovation gap is worsened by the lack of economic incentives for large pharmaceutical companies to develop new antibiotics, placing increasing pressure
papers.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
papers.summary: This review examines how machine learning is being applied across the antibiotic discovery pipeline, from initial small-molecule screening through pre-clinical optimization, in response to the escalating antimicrobial resistance crisis. It frames the urgency with epidemiological projections (rising from 4.71 million associated deaths in 2021 toward 8.22 million by 2050) and highlights the sparse antibacterial pipeline and weak economic incentives driving the need for computational approaches to accelerate discovery of compounds with novel mechanisms of action.

papers.title: Advancing the Alzheimer's disease research and care pipeline with agentic artificial intelligence: Opportunities, challenges, and priorities from the international clinical trials on Alzheimer's disease (CTAD) task force.
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds unprecedented potential to transform the entire Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias (ADRD) research and care continuum. During the 2025 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference, the CTAD Task Force reviewed recent advances in the field, highlighting the emerging role of agentic AI, and discussed priorities to guide future AI-driven innovation in ADRD. Agentic AI co-scientists are emerging as transformative tools to accelerate scientific discovery by autonomously integrating multimodal data, generating and evaluating new hypotheses, and c
papers.journal: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
papers.summary: This CTAD Task Force position paper reviews how agentic AI—AI systems that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks—could transform Alzheimer's disease and related dementias research and care, from data integration and hypothesis generation to trial design and clinical workflows. It outlines opportunities, challenges, and priority recommendations to guide responsible AI-driven innovation across the ADRD pipeline.

papers.title: Bridging traditional knowledge and modern technology: In-silico ethnopharmacology in herbal drug discovery.
papers.abstract: The use of herbal medicines and phytochemicals has gained considerable attention due to their structural diversity, selective toxicity, lower incidence of adverse effects, and affordability compared to conventional chemotherapy. Nevertheless, their precise mechanisms of action and bioactive constituents remain insufficiently understood, limiting their clinical translation and highlighting the need for rigorous scientific investigation. This review provides an integrative perspective on herbal-based drug discovery, beginning with the intersection of traditional disease classification systems, s
papers.journal: Journal of Ayurveda and integrative medicine
papers.summary: This review discusses how computational (in-silico) methods can be integrated with traditional ethnopharmacological knowledge to accelerate herbal drug discovery. It highlights that while phytochemicals offer structural diversity and favorable safety profiles, their mechanisms and active constituents remain poorly understood, limiting clinical translation. The authors advocate for rigorous scientific investigation combining traditional disease classification with modern computational approaches.

papers.title: BioLM-Score: Language-Prior Conditioned Probabilistic Geometric Potentials for Protein-Ligand Scoring.
papers.abstract: Protein-ligand scoring must address affinity prediction, pose selection, and virtual screening, but these objectives are not necessarily optimized together. Geometric likelihood models may generalize poorly when training-set structural coverage is limited. We test whether pretrained biomolecular representations improve scoring under a controlled geometric baseline.
papers.summary: The paper introduces BioLM-Score, a protein-ligand scoring method that conditions geometric probabilistic potentials on pretrained biomolecular language model representations. The authors test whether these language-model priors improve scoring performance over a controlled geometric baseline across affinity prediction, pose selection, and virtual screening tasks. The work probes whether pretrained representations can mitigate poor generalization of geometric likelihood models when structural training coverage is limited.

papers.title: A Machine Learning-Enhanced Ligand-Based Workflow Identifies Novel Cryptosporidium parvum Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Cryptosporidium parasites are a leading cause of waterborne disease worldwide, causing life-threatening diarrhea and malnutrition in young children and people with HIV. Currently, nitazoxanide is the only FDA-approved treatment, but it is largely ineffective in severely immunocompromised patients, highlighting the need for new therapies. Here, we use a ligand-based virtual screening workflow that integrates Thompson Sampling, a pharmacophore model, and a machine learning classifier to screen a subset of Enamine's REAL database comprising 51 million virtual compounds. Across two screening campa
papers.summary: The authors developed a ligand-based virtual screening workflow combining Thompson Sampling, a pharmacophore model, and a machine learning classifier to search 51 million virtual compounds for new Cryptosporidium parvum inhibitors. This approach identified novel candidate compounds targeting the parasite that causes severe diarrheal disease, addressing the urgent need for alternatives to the poorly effective nitazoxanide.

papers.title: Drug Repurposing in Pre-Eclampsia: Maternal Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Considerations for Clinical Trial Design.
papers.abstract: Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy affecting 3-8% of pregnancies worldwide, with no disease-modifying therapy currently available. Drug repurposing offers a promising strategy, yet no candidate has been validated to date. Pregnancy-associated physiological changes alter drug pharmacokinetics (PK), and pre-eclampsia itself may further modify drug disposition, complicating dose selection and contributing to inconclusive clinical trial outcomes. A structured literature search identified six prospective or randomized controlled trials of repurposed drugs for established pre-ecla
papers.summary: This review examines why drug repurposing trials for pre-eclampsia have so far failed to identify a disease-modifying therapy, focusing on how pregnancy-related physiological changes and pre-eclampsia itself alter drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. The authors argue that these PK/PD considerations are often overlooked in trial design, leading to suboptimal dosing and inconclusive results, and they outline how future trials should account for them.

papers.title: Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase d
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: This preprint benchmarks protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction methods on their ability to predict mutation-dependent drug responses, using deep mutational scanning data for the MET kinase across 11 inhibitor conditions. The authors find that these models struggle to generalize beyond their training sets when small mutations cause large changes in inhibitor sensitivity, highlighting a key limitation for computational drug discovery.

papers.title: Who Knows Medicinal Chemistry? Expertise, Attrition, and the Dissolving Boundaries of a Craft.
papers.abstract: Medicinal chemistry treats expertise as something one possesses or lacks, and arranges people accordingly. Yet the knowledge is largely tacit, its outcomes are dominated by attrition, and its boundaries are dissolving as new modalities, AI, and cross-organizational work draw other disciplines into design. This Viewpoint offers a more defensible measure of expertise.
papers.summary: This Viewpoint argues that medicinal chemistry expertise is largely tacit and poorly captured by binary possess-or-lack judgments, especially given high attrition in drug design outcomes. The author proposes a more defensible way to measure expertise as the field's boundaries blur with new modalities, AI, and cross-organizational collaboration.

papers.title: Democratizing Drug Discovery: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Massive Specific Protein Target QSAR Modeling Using ChEMBL.
papers.abstract: The proprietary nature of AI/ML tools in drug discovery limits access to advanced virtual screening methodologies. To address this, we present an open-source, automated pipeline for large-scale Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling utilizing ChEMBL. Our batch processing system constructed 2263 predictive models across multiple protein targets, applying both regression and classification strategies with strict quality control thresholds. The pipeline integrates ErG and RDKit descriptor families, employs Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms with Optuna-based hyperparameter
papers.summary: The authors present an open-source, automated pipeline that builds QSAR models at scale using ChEMBL data, generating 2263 target-specific predictive models with regression and classification approaches. The pipeline combines ErG and RDKit descriptors with Random Forest and XGBoost, using Optuna for hyperparameter tuning and strict quality-control thresholds. This work aims to democratize AI-driven virtual screening by providing a freely available, reproducible alternative to proprietary tools.

papers.title: Drug Design and Discovery: The Long Road From Hansch Analysis to Artificial Intelligence.
papers.abstract: The present article traces the long journey of the historical evolution and transformation of QSAR from its early days to its current role in drug discovery. It begins with the breakthrough created by the introduction of data analysis and highlights the major advances achieved throughout its development. Changes in molecular representation resulted in an explosion of molecular descriptors, while the rapid accumulation of large amounts of data demanded the application of elaborated statistical techniques. Today, machine learning and artificial intelligence have become integral components of pha
papers.summary: This review traces the historical evolution of QSAR (quantitative structure-activity relationships) from Hansch analysis to modern machine learning and AI-driven drug discovery. It highlights how changes in molecular representation led to an explosion of descriptors and how big data demanded sophisticated statistical techniques. The article positions machine learning and AI as integral components of contemporary pharmaceutical research.

papers.title: A Hybrid Ligand- and Structure-Based Drug Design Invoked through Square Attention in Protein-Ligand Transformer.
papers.abstract: Computer-aided molecular design based on evaluation of protein-ligand (PL) binding affinity is important for accelerating drug discovery. A deep-learning model for natural language processing (NLP) involving an attention mechanism (i.e., Transformer) is expected to improve the PL-affinity evaluation along with clarifying amino acid residues and ligand atoms that are responsible for molecular interactions. However, the original attention (i.e., a scaled dot-product with row-wise Softmax normalization) is an adapted method for relationships between homogeneous inputs (e.g., two sentences in the
papers.summary: This paper introduces a protein-ligand Transformer model that uses a novel 'square attention' mechanism to jointly evaluate binding affinity and identify the specific amino acid residues and ligand atoms driving molecular interactions. The approach combines ligand-based and structure-based drug design principles within a single deep-learning framework, aiming to improve both predictive accuracy and interpretability compared to standard attention mechanisms adapted from NLP.

papers.title: CB-Smart: A Cloud-Based Machine Learning Platform for Screening Cannabinoid Receptor Ligands.
papers.abstract: Cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 are class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) implicated in pain modulation, neuroinflammation, immune regulation, and metabolic processes, making them important therapeutic targets. Conventional structure-based virtual screening for cannabinoid ligands remains computationally intensive and limited in throughput. To overcome this challenge, this work presents CB-Smart, a cloud-enabled machine learning (ML) platform to predict binding of ligands and their relative binding affinity to CB1 and CB2. Using curated experimentally validated ligands and GPCR decoy d
papers.summary: CB-Smart is a cloud-based machine learning platform that predicts whether a small molecule binds the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 and estimates its relative binding affinity. It was trained on curated experimentally validated ligands and GPCR decoys, offering a faster, higher-throughput alternative to conventional structure-based virtual screening for cannabinoid drug discovery.

papers.title: GPCRAgent: an intelligent multi-agent platform integrating knowledge graphs and large language models for GPCR-targeted drug discovery.
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major therapeutic targets in drug discovery. However, systematic characterization of GPCR functions and ligand interactions remains constrained by the high cost and complexity of experimental approaches. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in biomedical question answering, their direct application to GPCR research is limited by insufficient integration of structured domain knowledge and poor interpretability of generated inferences.
papers.summary: GPCRAgent is a multi-agent platform that combines knowledge graphs with large language models to support GPCR-targeted drug discovery. It addresses the limitations of standalone LLMs by integrating structured domain knowledge and improving the interpretability of inferences. The platform aims to enable more systematic characterization of GPCR functions and ligand interactions without relying solely on costly experimental methods.

papers.title: QRxVision: Multimodal QR Encoding and Computer Vision for Domain-Specific Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Computational approaches applied to the drug discovery pipeline are invaluable because of their overall speed or time to solution, sustainability, accessibility combined with ever improving accuracy. Furthermore, the high-throughput virtual screening supports practical sampling of the vast chemical space for target-relevant bioactive compounds that can be experimentally validated further downstream in the drug development process. The current paradigm being practiced in computer-aided drug screening strategies centers around structure-based and ligand-based approaches supported by a range of c
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: QRxVision introduces a multimodal framework that combines QR-code-style encoding of molecular data with computer vision models to support domain-specific drug discovery tasks. The approach aims to make high-throughput virtual screening more accessible and efficient by representing chemical information in a format amenable to image-based machine learning. It extends existing structure- and ligand-based screening paradigms with a novel encoding strategy.

papers.title: Phenylpropanoid Amides from Buteae monospermae Semen as Hepcidin-Modulating Candidates for Anemia of Inflammation: Network Pharmacology, Deep Learning Prediction, and In Vitro Validation.
papers.abstract: Anemia of inflammation (AI) is largely driven by interleukin-6 (IL-6)-induced hepcidin overproduction, which disrupts systemic iron homeostasis. Buteae monospermae Semen (BMS), the seeds of Butea monosperma (Lam.) Kuntze and a traditional Tibetan medicine, has long been used for blood-related disorders, yet its active constituents against AI remain unclear. Here, an integrated strategy combining ADMET screening, network pharmacology, deep learning-based affinity prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and in vitro validation was applied to 58 BMS-derived compounds. Forty-
papers.summary: This study integrates ADMET screening, network pharmacology, deep learning-based affinity prediction, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics with in vitro validation to identify phenylpropanoid amides from Butea monosperma seeds as candidate hepcidin-modulating compounds for treating anemia of inflammation. The work highlights a computational-to-experimental pipeline for natural product drug discovery targeting IL-6-driven hepcidin overproduction.

papers.title: GAC-BiT-CNN: A Hybrid Generative Adversarial Capsule-Transformer-CNN Model with Fused Protein Language Model Embeddings for Methyltransferase Prediction.
papers.abstract: Methyltransferases (MTs) are a functionally diverse class of enzymes that catalyse methyl group transfer from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to DNA, RNA, and proteins, thereby regulating epigenetic programming, gene expression, and numerous disease processes. Dysregulation of these enzymes is implicated in a wide spectrum of human cancers and neurodegenerative disorders, making their accurate computational identification a priority in both basic research and drug discovery. We present GAC-BiT-CNN, a novel hybrid deep learning framework integrating Generative Adversarial Capsule Networks (GAC),
papers.summary: The authors present GAC-BiT-CNN, a hybrid deep learning framework that combines generative adversarial capsule networks, a bidirectional transformer, and a CNN to predict methyltransferases from protein language model embeddings. The model aims to improve computational identification of this enzyme class, which is relevant to epigenetics, cancer, and drug discovery. The abstract describes the architecture but does not report performance results.

papers.title: Integrated Biochemical and Computational Evaluation of Bis-Imidazolium Derivatives 3e-3g in Cholinesterase and HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Assays.
papers.abstract: Bis-imidazolium derivatives (3e, 3f, 3g) were evaluated for their inhibitory activity against acetylcholinesterase (AChE), butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), and human immunodeficiency virus type 1 reverse transcriptase (HIV-1 RT) using colorimetric assays and molecular docking. For the HIV-1 RT-3e complex, a 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) analysis were performed. Compound 3e emerged as the most active derivative, showing the lowest half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values: 13.36 µg/mL for AChE, 4.95 µg/mL for BCh
papers.summary: This study evaluated three bis-imidazolium derivatives (3e, 3f, 3g) for inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, and HIV-1 reverse transcriptase using colorimetric assays and molecular docking. Compound 3e was the most potent, with IC50 values of 13.36 µg/mL for AChE and 4.95 µg/mL for BChE, and its complex with HIV-1 RT was further examined by 100 ns molecular dynamics and MM/GBSA analysis. The work combines experimental enzyme assays with computational modeling to characterize these dual-target compounds.

papers.title: A TLR4-Associated Microglia-Endothelial Inflammatory Axis in Drug-Resistant Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: Integrated Transcriptomic and Genetic Evidence.
papers.abstract: Microglia-driven neuroinflammation contributes to epileptogenesis and drug resistance in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), but the cellular organization of the neuroinflammatory hub and its coupling to the cerebrovascular endothelium remain unresolved. We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of publicly available datasets, integrating paired hippocampal bulk transcriptomics (GSE134697), an integrated temporal-lobe single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) atlas (9 patients with drug-resistant TLE and 4 controls), two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and summary-based Mendelian r
papers.summary: This study integrates public hippocampal bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets with Mendelian randomization to identify a microglia-endothelial inflammatory axis linked to TLR4 in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. The findings suggest that microglia-driven neuroinflammation couples with cerebrovascular endothelial cells, and genetic evidence supports a causal role for TLR4-associated pathways. The work is a secondary analysis of existing data, so experimental validation is still needed.

papers.title: How Reliable Is In Silico ADMET Profiling? A Comparison of Tools Complementing Experimental In Vitro Analyses of Newly Developed Breast Cancer Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: In silico analyses, including absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) profiling and drug-likeness evaluations, constitute powerful tools in modern drug discovery. These computational methods enable high-throughput screening of molecular libraries to assess therapeutic potential while identifying unfavourable pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiles early in the development process. To bridge the gap between computational models and empirical data, this study evaluates the reliability and limitations of predictive ADMET profiling by comparing in silico outputs ac
papers.summary: This study benchmarks several in silico ADMET prediction tools against experimental in vitro data for newly developed breast cancer therapeutics, assessing how well computational predictions match empirical pharmacokinetic and toxicity measurements. The authors identify strengths and limitations of current ADMET models, highlighting where computational predictions diverge from experimental results. The work provides practical guidance on the reliability of in silico profiling in early drug discovery.

papers.title: Anticancer activity of sodium propionate in hepatocellular carcinoma cells via downregulation of HDAC2 and HDAC6.
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is an aggressive malignancy driven by epigenetic dysregulation. This study investigates the anticancer potential of sodium propionate (SP) as an epigenetic modulator targeting histone deacetylases (HDACs) using an integrated in silico and in vitro approach. Bioinformatics analyses were conducted using publicly available HCC transcriptomic datasets from GEO database, disease gene database (GeneCards database), and chemical-gene interaction networks (Comparative Toxicogenomic Database) to identify potential therapeutic targets, HDAC2 and HDAC6 as key therapeutic ta
papers.summary: This study uses bioinformatics analysis of public HCC transcriptomic and toxicogenomic datasets to identify HDAC2 and HDAC6 as key targets of sodium propionate, a short-chain fatty acid with epigenetic-modulating activity. In vitro experiments in hepatocellular carcinoma cells support that sodium propionate exerts anticancer effects via downregulation of these HDACs. The work combines computational target prediction with cell-based validation to propose a repurposable metabolite for HCC.

papers.title: Prediction of Molecular Physicochemical Properties Using Molecular Structure and Characteristics.
papers.abstract: The prediction of molecular physicochemical properties-such as solubility, hydration free energy, and lipophilicity-plays a crucial role in multiple fields, including drug discovery and materials science. Current prediction methods predominantly fall into two categories: machine learning methods based on molecular descriptors and deep learning methods that learn representations directly from molecular structures. However, when evaluated under rigorous scaffold splitting, these methods often exhibit limited generalization capability, resulting in unsatisfactory prediction accuracy. In this stud
papers.summary: This study addresses the limited generalization of current molecular property prediction methods under rigorous scaffold splitting by proposing an approach that combines molecular structure with additional molecular characteristics. The work targets key physicochemical properties like solubility, hydration free energy, and lipophilicity, which are important for drug discovery and materials science. The abstract is truncated, so the specific methodological details and performance gains are not fully described.

papers.title: Fast, lightweight BBB permeability predictions for molecular design.
papers.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a selectively permeable border that regulates the transport of chemical compounds into and out of the central nervous system (CNS). To discover medicinal drugs that can target the CNS, we must be able to efficiently screen pools of potential candidate CNS-targeting drugs to identify those that can permeate the BBB. However, drugs that readily permeate the BBB are comparatively rare, thus CNS drug discovery typically requires screening very large candidate libraries. In the last two decades, a diverse portfolio of machine learning models has been developed to pr
papers.summary: This paper presents a fast, lightweight machine learning approach for predicting blood-brain barrier permeability, addressing the need to efficiently screen large candidate libraries in CNS drug discovery. The method aims to identify compounds likely to permeate the BBB without the computational overhead of more complex models. It offers a practical screening tool for molecular design pipelines targeting central nervous system therapeutics.

papers.title: A trustworthy semantic knowledge network linking data-driven cell phenotypes to diseases and drugs.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association and other genetic studies have identified genes involved in disease pathogenesis, and their encoded proteins have provided therapeutic targets. However, little is known about which cells are the functional home of these disease-associated genes and proteins. Single-cell technologies are enabling high-resolution profiling of cell phenotypes and revealing cellular contexts of disease, yet much of the resulting knowledge remains embedded in individual datasets and scientific literature. To address these gaps, the National Library of Medicine has developed Cell Knowledge Ne
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: The National Library of Medicine has developed Cell Knowledge Network, a semantic knowledge graph that integrates data-driven cell phenotypes from single-cell studies with information about diseases and drugs. This resource aims to connect disease-associated genes and proteins to the specific cell types where they function, making scattered single-cell knowledge more accessible and interoperable.

papers.title: Atractylenolide II Alleviates 5-Fluorouracil-Induced Intestinal Toxicity Through Potentially Targeting the TLR4-Mediated MYD88/NF-κB Signaling Pathway: An Integrated In Silico and In Vitro Study.
papers.abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a potent compound in anti-tumor chemotherapy; however, its clinical utility is hampered by dose-limiting intestinal toxicity. Atractylenolide II (AT-II), a bioactive sesquiterpene derived from Atractylodis Rhizoma, has reported anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective activities. In this study, we employed an integrated strategy combining chemical characterization, computational pharmacology, and in vitro experiments to investigate the protective effect of AT-II against 5-FU-induced intestinal toxicity and clarify its potential target-associated mechanism. UHPLC-QE-MS was
papers.summary: This study investigates whether Atractylenolide II (AT-II), a compound from the herb Atractylodis Rhizoma, can protect intestinal cells from toxicity caused by the chemotherapy drug 5-fluorouracil. Using computational target prediction combined with in vitro cell experiments, the authors propose that AT-II works by targeting TLR4 and dampening the MYD88/NF-κB inflammatory signaling pathway. The findings suggest a potential natural-product strategy to reduce 5-FU's dose-limiting gut side effects.

papers.title: Graphics processing unit-accelerated quantum simulation for molecular biology and drug discovery: algorithms, platforms, and emerging applications.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has intensified the need for methods that describe molecular systems with quantum-mechanical accuracy. Gate-based quantum computing offers a principled framework for simulating electronic structure, molecular interactions, and biological processes at a fidelity inaccessible to classical force fields or density functional theory alone, yet scarce, noisy hardware limits direct experimentation. Graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated quantum simulation has emerged as a practical bridge, allowing quantum algorithms to be developed, validated, and benchmarked on classical
papers.summary: This review surveys how GPUs can accelerate classical simulation of quantum algorithms for molecular biology and drug discovery, covering algorithms, platforms, and emerging applications. It argues that GPU-accelerated quantum simulation provides a practical bridge for developing and benchmarking quantum algorithms despite scarce, noisy quantum hardware.

papers.title: Biological and In Silico Evaluation of Two Nitrogen-Sulfur Heterocycles: Limited Cytotoxic, Antioxidant, and Antimicrobial Activities With Preliminary Anti-Inflammatory Effects.
papers.abstract: In this study, two nitrogen-sulfur-containing heterocyclic compounds, 9 and 10, were synthesized, and their biological activities were evaluated together with in silico prediction of selected ADME/T properties. Their cytotoxic effects were tested across multiple cancer cell lines and a noncancerous cell line, while antimicrobial activity was evaluated against bacterial and fungal strains. Antioxidant capacity was investigated using FRAP, DPPH, ABTS, and phosphomolybdenum assays. Preliminary anti-inflammatory effects were evaluated by measuring nitric oxide (NO) production and the expression of
papers.summary: Two new nitrogen-sulfur heterocyclic compounds were synthesized and tested across cancer cell lines, microbial strains, and antioxidant assays, with in silico ADME/T predictions and preliminary anti-inflammatory measurements. The compounds showed limited cytotoxic, antioxidant, and antimicrobial activity, with only preliminary evidence of anti-inflammatory effects. The study is largely a negative/incremental result with modest biological promise.

papers.title: Novel Thiochroman-4-one Derivatives Bearing a Thiosemicarbazide Scaffold With Potential Antioxidant, α-Glucosidase Inhibitory, and Antibacterial Activities.
papers.abstract: In this work, a series of novel thiochroman-4-one derivatives incorporating a thiosemicarbazide moiety were rationally designed and synthesized. In vitro bioactivity assays demonstrated that most target compounds exerted potent ABTS radical scavenging and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities. Notably, compound 6m exhibited superior bioactivities, with an IC50 value of 12.96 µM for ABTS radical scavenging and 27.48 µM for α-glucosidase inhibition, which were markedly stronger than those of the positive controls Trolox and acarbose, respectively. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics (M
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a series of thiochroman-4-one derivatives containing a thiosemicarbazide group and tested them for antioxidant, α-glucosidase inhibitory, and antibacterial activity. Compound 6m was the most potent, outperforming Trolox in ABTS radical scavenging (IC50 12.96 µM) and acarbose in α-glucosidase inhibition (IC50 27.48 µM), with docking and molecular dynamics simulations supporting the binding mode. This identifies a promising scaffold for further optimization as antioxidant and antidiabetic agents.

papers.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides.
papers.abstract: Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI - a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed a
papers.summary: Pepti-DrugPhAI is a multimodal AI tool that predicts pharmacokinetic properties and toxicity for peptide drug candidates, addressing a major bottleneck in peptide therapeutic development. It aims to be more comprehensive than existing solutions by covering a wide range of peptide compounds and integrating multiple data modalities.

papers.title: ML-QSAR and Fragment Selectivity for the Identification of Fourth-Generation EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to establish an integrative workflow that couples QSAR modeling based on ML-QSAR, fragment-level selectivity analysis, large-library virtual screening, and MD simulations to identify fourth-generation inhibitors of the EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S mutant. Independent XGBoost models were trained on curated ChEMBL bioactivity data for mutant and wild-type EGFR, yielding strong predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.74-0.81; RMSE = 0.53-0.56) together with interpretable SHAP feature attributions. Fragment analysis highlighted structural motifs that were subsequently used to screen the ZINC databas
papers.summary: This study combines machine-learning QSAR models, fragment-level selectivity analysis, large-scale virtual screening of the ZINC database, and molecular dynamics simulations to identify potential fourth-generation inhibitors targeting the EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S mutant EGFR. The XGBoost models achieved strong predictive accuracy (R² = 0.74–0.81) and provided interpretable SHAP feature attributions, while fragment analysis highlighted structural motifs used to guide screening. The work presents an integrative computational workflow for discovering mutant-selective EGFR inhibitors.

papers.title: Computer-Aided Drug Design for Immunosuppressive Tumor Microenvironment Reprogramming: A Critical Review.
papers.abstract: How can cellular interactions in solid tumors guide molecular interventions against immune suppression? This critical review examines how computer-aided drug design (CADD) connects immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) states to testable molecular hypotheses. We distinguish observational artificial intelligence (AI) predictions from molecular intervention hypotheses and examine the experimental evidence required to evaluate them. We reviewed patient-derived models, spatial and multi-omics profiling, molecular design, simulation, and pharmacology using literature identified through 15
papers.summary: This critical review examines how computer-aided drug design (CADD) can be used to reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in solid tumors. It distinguishes observational AI predictions from testable molecular intervention hypotheses and discusses the experimental evidence needed to validate them, drawing on patient-derived models, spatial and multi-omics profiling, molecular design, simulation, and pharmacology.

papers.title: Virtual Screening-Derived Computational Lead Candidates for MAO-B Inhibition in Parkinson's Disease: Pathway-Informed Docking, Molecular Dynamics, DFT and ADMET Evaluation.
papers.abstract: Monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) is a clinically validated target in Parkinson's disease (PD), but docking rank alone is insufficient to establish a CNS-directed inhibitor. We integrated MAOB-related pathway context, domain-resolved structural annotation, GNINA virtual screening, predicted blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeation, molecular dynamics (MD), density functional theory (DFT) and ADMET assessment to nominate hypothesis-stage computational candidates. A pharmacophore-derived input collection 2870 entries was subjected to virtual screening; a curated BBB-positive, favorable Vina/CNN-affinity s
papers.summary: This study integrates pathway context, GNINA virtual screening, blood-brain barrier prediction, molecular dynamics, DFT, and ADMET profiling to nominate computational lead candidates for MAO-B inhibition in Parkinson's disease. Starting from a 2870-compound library, the authors prioritize candidates with favorable docking and CNN affinity plus predicted CNS penetration, then validate stability and electronic properties in silico. The work is a hypothesis-generating computational pipeline rather than experimental validation of new inhibitors.

papers.title: Emerging Computational Advances in Simulating PCSK9 Variant Dynamics for Therapeutic Design Against Hypercholesterolemia.
papers.abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a premier model for precision medicine, having moved from genetic discovery to approved therapeutics within two decades. Yet despite the clinical success of monoclonal antibodies, small interfering RNA and the newly approved oral macrocyclic-peptide inhibitor class, targeting PCSK9 remains a demanding biophysical challenge. Clinical translation has concentrated almost entirely on the rigid, well-resolved subtilisin-like catalytic domain that interfaces with the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). By contrast, the C-terminal cysteine
papers.summary: This review surveys computational approaches for simulating how PCSK9 variants behave structurally and dynamically, with the goal of informing therapeutic design against hypercholesterolemia. It highlights that clinical translation has focused almost exclusively on the rigid catalytic domain that binds LDLR, while the flexible C-terminal cysteine-rich domain remains underexplored as a target. The paper argues that emerging simulation methods could open new avenues for variant-aware drug design against PCSK9.

papers.title: Discovery of Two Potential and Novel Toll-like Receptor 7 Antagonists via Molecular Docking, Molecular Dynamics Simulation and In Vitro Biological Evaluation.
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is an important pattern recognition receptor. It mainly participates in the recognition of single-stranded RNA and is closely related to various disease processes. In humans, the enormous potential of TLR7 antagonists in reducing inflammation and alleviating autoimmune damage has been identified. Similar effects have also been observed in livestock and poultry. Therefore, using porcine TLR7 as the target, we combined virtual screening with a heterologous reporter gene assay to identify potential ligands, aiming to provide a research basis for the development of immu
papers.summary: This study used molecular docking and dynamics simulations to virtually screen compounds against porcine Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7), then validated hits with an in vitro reporter gene assay. Two novel TLR7 antagonists were identified, offering starting points for developing anti-inflammatory or immunomodulatory agents, particularly for livestock applications.

papers.title: HierL2GDTA: Hierarchical Interaction Modeling with Local and Global Features for Drug-Target Affinity Prediction.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-target binding affinity is essential for drug discovery. However, existing methods face limitations in capturing local and global molecular features and in effectively integrating protein and ligand representations for interaction modeling. Here, we present HierL2GDTA, a sequence-based hierarchical framework for predicting binding affinity. Pretrained protein and molecular representations are processed by multi-scale convolutions to extract local features, followed by a bidirectional gated recurrent unit and dilated convolutions to capture broader protein and ligand
papers.summary: HierL2GDTA is a sequence-based deep learning framework for predicting drug-target binding affinity that combines pretrained protein and molecular representations with multi-scale convolutions to capture local features, followed by bidirectional GRU and dilated convolutions for broader context. The hierarchical design aims to better integrate ligand and protein representations for interaction modeling, addressing limitations of prior methods in capturing both local and global molecular features.

papers.title: A Machine-Learning Framework Integrating Frequency-Domain Spectral Features for Ligand Classification and Candidate Prioritization.
papers.abstract: AI-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) combines molecular modeling with machine learning to support lead identification and candidate prioritization. Conventional molecular descriptors principally encode static chemical structures, leaving frequency-domain behavior as an additional source of molecular information. We therefore developed the terahertz fusion descriptor (THz-FD), a feature-fusion framework that integrates terahertz (THz) frequency-domain features for Na+/K+-ATPase ligand classification and retrospective ranking. Extra Trees (ET), Random Forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM) c
papers.summary: The authors developed THz-FD, a machine-learning framework that fuses conventional molecular descriptors with terahertz frequency-domain spectral features to classify Na+/K+-ATPase ligands and prioritize drug candidates. Using Extra Trees, Random Forest, and SVM classifiers, they show that adding frequency-domain information improves ligand classification and retrospective ranking compared to static descriptors alone.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence with High-Throughput Biological Testing for Antimicrobial Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is eroding the effectiveness of existing antibiotics, while conventional discovery continues to yield few clinically useful chemical classes. This critical narrative review evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI) has been integrated with high-throughput screening (HTS) and prospective biological testing in antibacterial discovery. Graph-based and generative models have produced prospectively confirmed active compounds, pathogen-selective candidates and structures outside familiar antibacterial scaffolds. Where studies included suitable comparators, AI-guided selecti
papers.summary: This review examines how AI has been integrated with high-throughput screening and prospective biological testing in antibacterial drug discovery. It finds that graph-based and generative models have produced prospectively confirmed active compounds, pathogen-selective candidates, and structures outside familiar antibacterial scaffolds, though the abstract is truncated before full comparative conclusions. The work highlights AI's promise for revitalizing antibiotic discovery amid antimicrobial resistance.

papers.title: Navigating the Pharma 4.0 revolution: how AI-enabled applications and predictive modelling shaped pharmaceutical development in the post-pandemic era: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Pharma 4.0 is touted to make processes more efficient and resilient to unforeseen circumstances, boosting productivity, speed and accuracy of pharmaceutical systems. Besides operational stability, these technological implementations could potentially improve clinical outcomes. AI-enabled Pharma 4.0 applications and predictive modelling are utilised in pharmaceutical development for the discovery of new compounds that could potentially be used as drugs for COVID-19. This systematic review examined how contemporary Pharma 4.0 technologies have impacted pharmaceutical development in the post COVI
papers.summary: This systematic review examines how AI-enabled Pharma 4.0 technologies and predictive modelling have influenced pharmaceutical development in the post-COVID era, with particular attention to drug discovery for COVID-19. The authors synthesize evidence on how these implementations improve process efficiency, resilience, and productivity, and discuss their potential to enhance clinical outcomes. The review highlights both operational benefits and the role of AI in accelerating compound discovery.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Multifaceted Toolkit for Antibacterial Drug Discovery against Resistance.
papers.abstract: How artificial intelligence (AI) can be rationally applied to antibacterial drug discovery and development to overcome antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains insufficiently defined, particularly across different resistance mechanisms and translational stages. The global emergence and dissemination of AMR are compromising conventional antibacterial therapies, while slow antibiotic discovery, limited target diversity, and reliance on single-mechanism drug design further increase the risk of inadequate treatment options. With strengths in multi-omics integration, complex pattern recognition, and
papers.summary: This review argues that AI can serve as an integrated toolkit across the antibacterial drug discovery pipeline, from target identification to clinical translation, to counter antimicrobial resistance. It emphasizes AI's strengths in multi-omics integration and complex pattern recognition to address slow discovery, limited target diversity, and single-mechanism drug design. The paper frames AI application explicitly across different resistance mechanisms and translational stages.

papers.title: Computational drug screening for drug-resistant tuberculosis: advances, challenges, and future perspectives.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches-including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks-have substantially expande
papers.summary: This review examines computational approaches for discovering new drugs against drug-resistant tuberculosis, including virtual screening, AI-driven modeling, and hybrid frameworks. It highlights how these methods have expanded the search for anti-TB agents but also discusses remaining challenges and future directions. The paper is a broad overview rather than a primary research study.

papers.title: Multitarget docking and toxicity-guided prioritisation of phytochemicals from Bangladeshi medicinal plants against wheat fungal pathogens.
papers.abstract: The rising issue of fungicide resistance, along with environmental concerns related to synthetic fungicides, highlights the need for safer and more sustainable antifungal agents. In this computational study, we screened nineteen phytochemicals from locally available medicinal plants in Bangladesh against three fungal protein targets associated with major wheat diseases: class I sesquiterpene synthase (PDB ID: 8H4P) and trichothecene 3-O-acetyltransferase (TRI101; PDB ID: 3B2S) from Fusarium graminearum, and the AvrSr50 effector protein (PDB ID: 7MQQ) from Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. Blin
papers.summary: This computational study screened nineteen phytochemicals from Bangladeshi medicinal plants against three fungal protein targets linked to major wheat diseases (Fusarium graminearum and Puccinia graminis). Using multitarget molecular docking combined with toxicity-guided prioritisation, the authors identify candidate plant-derived compounds with potential antifungal activity. The work is purely in silico and provides a starting point for experimental validation of natural-product fungicides.

papers.title: A knowledge graph-driven literature-based discovery framework for drug repurposing in aplastic anaemia.
papers.abstract: Aplastic anaemia is a haematological disorder characterized by immune-mediated destruction of haematopoietic stem cells and bone marrow failure. Although immunosuppressive therapies are currently used, their lack of target specificity underscores the need for systematic approaches to identify precise therapeutic targets and explore drug repurposing opportunities.
papers.summary: The authors present a knowledge graph-based literature discovery framework aimed at finding drug repurposing candidates for aplastic anaemia, a rare immune-mediated bone marrow failure disorder. By integrating literature-derived relationships into a knowledge graph, the approach seeks to identify precise therapeutic targets beyond current non-specific immunosuppressive therapies. The abstract describes the framework's motivation and design but does not report specific validated drug candidates or outcomes.

papers.title: Immediate early response 3 promotes airway epithelial inflammation and represents a therapeutic target in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by persistent airway inflammation, yet clinically useful biomarkers and mechanistically validated therapeutic targets remain limited. Here, we aimed to identify and functionally validate smoke-responsive regulators of airway epithelial inflammation in COPD and establish an interpretable prediction framework by integrating population-based clinical data, multi-omics analyses, genetic causal inference, and experimental validation.
papers.summary: This study identifies the gene IER3 as a smoke-responsive driver of airway epithelial inflammation in COPD, using an integrated approach combining population clinical data, multi-omics, genetic causal inference, and experimental validation. The authors propose IER3 as both a potential biomarker and a therapeutic target, and build an interpretable prediction framework for COPD.

papers.title: Identification and structural characterization of MMP1 and MMP9 as potential targets of curcumin and resveratrol in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a major subtype of lung cancer characterized by substantial molecular heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Curcumin and resveratrol are naturally occurring bioactive compounds with reported anticancer activities, but their potential molecular targets and mechanisms in LUAD remain incompletely characterized.
papers.summary: This study uses computational approaches to identify MMP1 and MMP9 as potential molecular targets of the natural compounds curcumin and resveratrol in lung adenocarcinoma, then structurally characterizes these interactions. The work suggests a possible mechanistic basis for the reported anticancer effects of these polyphenols in LUAD, though the findings are based on in silico prediction rather than experimental validation.

papers.title: Investigating the Protective Role of Folic Acid in Fluoride-Induced Neurotoxicity: An Integrative Computational and In Vivo Study.
papers.abstract: Excessive fluoride exposure has been associated with neurotoxicity, including cognitive deficits and an increased risk of dementia. SIRT1, a key regulator of oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammation, is downregulated in fluoride-induced neurotoxicity. This study aimed to identify a potential nutraceutical compound that modulates SIRT1 and explore its effects in a rat model of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity.
papers.summary: This study used computational screening to identify folic acid as a potential modulator of SIRT1, a protein downregulated in fluoride-induced neurotoxicity, and then tested it in a rat model. The in vivo experiments suggest that folic acid may protect against fluoride-induced neurotoxicity, likely through SIRT1-related pathways involving oxidative stress and inflammation.

papers.title: Cardioprotective Potential of Fagonia arabica Phytochemicals Against Adrenaline-Induced Myocardial Infarction: Insights From Computational and Experimental Studies.
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a primary cause of cardiovascular death around the world; single-target conventional treatments remain inadequate and have adverse effects.
papers.summary: This study investigates whether phytochemicals from the plant Fagonia arabica can protect against adrenaline-induced myocardial infarction, combining computational docking and network analysis with experimental validation. The authors identify candidate compounds and propose multi-target mechanisms, supporting the plant's traditional cardioprotective use. The work is preliminary and relies on an animal model, so clinical relevance remains to be established.

papers.title: AI-enabled drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease: from computational nomination to pharmacological proof.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale and speed of drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcriptomic signature matching, network-based systems pharmacology, real-world data pharmacoepidemiology and multi-omics machine learning have generated hundreds of candidate drugs, while repurposed agents account for 35% (56 of 158) of drugs and 42% (15 of 36) of Phase 3 agents in the 2026 AD pipeline. Clinical translation, however, remains unproven. Randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists illustrate the gap between prioritisation and therapeutic proof: semaglutide did not sl
papers.summary: This review surveys how AI methods—transcriptomic signature matching, network pharmacology, real-world pharmacoepidemiology, and multi-omics machine learning—have generated hundreds of candidate repurposed drugs for Alzheimer's disease, with repurposed agents now comprising 35% of the 2026 AD pipeline and 42% of Phase 3 agents. However, the authors emphasize that clinical translation remains unproven, citing GLP-1 receptor agonist trials (e.g., semaglutide) as evidence of the gap between computational prioritization and pharmacological proof.

papers.title: Structure-Based Discovery of Coumarin-Triazole Derivatives Targeting the Conserved QGDNQ Motif of Chandipura RdRp.
papers.abstract: Chandipura virus (CHPV) is a recently discovered neurotropic virus associated with severe encephalitis in children and for which there is currently no specific antiviral treatment. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) is an attractive antiviral target because of its essential role in viral RNA synthesis and the presence of conserved catalytic motifs required for polymerase function. In this study, a structure-based computational approach was employed to investigate coumarin-triazole derivatives as potential inhibitors targeting the conserved QGDNQ motif-containing region of CHPV RdRp.
papers.summary: This study uses computational structure-based methods to identify coumarin-triazole derivatives as potential inhibitors of the Chandipura virus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, targeting its conserved QGDNQ catalytic motif. The work is preliminary and in silico only, with no experimental validation reported in the abstract.

papers.title: Targeting IL-1R1 and androgen receptor using natural compounds from Aconitum heterophyllum and Podophyllum hexandrum: an in silico and in vitro study.
papers.abstract: Lung and prostate cancers remain leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, driven by inflammation-mediated tumour progression and hormone-dependent signalling. IL-1R1 promotes chronic inflammation, metastasis, and tumour survival, while androgen receptor (AR) signalling is a central driver of prostate cancer growth. Simultaneous targeting of inflammatory and androgenic pathways represents a promising strategy to overcome therapeutic resistance.
papers.summary: This study uses computational docking and in vitro assays to identify natural compounds from two medicinal plants (Aconitum heterophyllum and Podophyllum hexandrum) that can simultaneously inhibit IL-1R1 (an inflammation receptor) and the androgen receptor (AR), two proteins implicated in lung and prostate cancer progression. The authors propose that dual targeting of inflammatory and hormone signaling pathways could help overcome therapeutic resistance, though the abstract does not report specific compound identities or quantitative results.
